name: Human placentophagy

lead: Human placentophagy is the postpartum eating of the placenta, most often as dehydrated, encapsulated pills but also raw, cooked or in smoothies. Followers say it restores energy, improves mood, supports milk supply and speeds recovery, which they connect with feeling and looking more vital after birth.

The practice is common in other mammals and has been growing among women in Western countries, while cross-cultural surveys find no traditional human culture that routinely eats it. Reviews describe the evidence of benefit as anecdotal or self-reported, and a small randomized pilot found no salivary hormone differences from placebo.

paras: A person or specialist prepares the placenta, usually by steaming and dehydrating it and encapsulating it, and the capsules are taken in the postpartum weeks. Alternatives include tinctures, smoothies and cooked dishes.

The CDC reported a newborn infection with group B Streptococcus linked to maternal placenta capsules, and the CDC and ACOG advise against the practice. Studies note that processing does not reliably remove bacteria and that preparation is unregulated.

angle.text: Followers take placenta pills to feel more energetic and recover faster after childbirth, which they link to looking rested and healthy. Evidence of such benefit has not been shown in controlled studies.

lead: Placentophagy, also called placentophagia, is eating the placenta after birth. It is widespread among mammals, though a cross-cultural survey of 179 human societies found no tradition of routinely eating it. [1][2]

Interest has grown among postpartum women in the United States and other Western countries. The most common method is steaming, dehydrating and encapsulating the placenta. Promoters claim physical and emotional benefits including mood stabilisation, recovery and milk production, and followers in wellness circles often describe it as a way to regain energy and vitality. [1][3]
Research consists of reviews, surveys and a small pilot trial. Reviews report no clinical benefit demonstrated, and health bodies advise against it. [1][4][5]

CDC and ACOG advise against capsules

paras: Preparations include raw, cooked, roasted, dehydrated, encapsulated, smoothie and tincture forms, with encapsulation after steaming and dehydration the most frequent. Numerous companies offer preparation services. [1]

A cross-cultural survey of 179 societies found a conspicuous absence of maternal placentophagy traditions. [2] Traditional Chinese medicine has used dried human placenta (ziheche) for conditions such as wasting disease, infertility and impotence, per Wikipedia. [6] A review describes the modern practice as growing among middle-class white women in Western societies. [3] Chef Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall cooked and ate placenta on a television programme, which drew criticism. [6]

Advocates say the placenta retains hormones and nutrients that help prevent postpartum depression, relieve pain, aid recovery and boost lactation. A survey by anthropologists at the University of South Florida and UNLV found about three-quarters of respondents who ate their own placenta reported positive experiences such as better mood, energy and lactation. [6][7]

A 2018 pilot randomized trial (27 participants) found no significant differences in salivary hormones between placenta and placebo groups beyond baseline differences. [8] A 2018 laboratory study of nine placentas examined how dehydration and steaming change hormones, trace elements and microbial contamination. [9] A 2015 review of ten articles (four human, six animal) found studies on lactation, uterine contraction and mood inconclusive. [4] A 2018 review reported no scientific evidence of clinical benefit and no placental hormones retained in helpful amounts after encapsulation. [1]

The CDC reported a newborn with group B Streptococcus infection likely linked to the mother's placenta capsules and advised avoiding them. [6] A 2025 review notes that ACOG and the CDC do not recommend the practice because the products are unregulated and carry bacterial and endocrine concerns. [5]
